diagnano|4430878431.findings: High-risk pregnancy findings (β-hCG 4,610 IU/L with no intrauterine gestational sac on ultrasound, left adnexal lesion, and moderate free fluid) plus minimal spotting and hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia) most strongly indicate ectopic pregnancy; concurrent diffuse vomiting/diarrhea with reported GI illness in relatives suggests gastroenteritis, while hypotension and tachycardia also require consideration of sepsis (though no measured fever and exam are less typical).

diagnano|dcb8985267.findings: Positive β-hCG (4610 IU/L) with ultrasound showing no intrauterine gestational sac, a left adnexal lesion, moderate free fluid, and minimal vaginal spotting with hypotension/tachycardia—most consistent with ruptured ectopic pregnancy; vomiting/diarrhea could mimic gastroenteritis but does not explain the pregnancy findings.

diagnano|62110e717a.findings: Positive β-hCG (4,610 IU/L) with ultrasound showing no intrauterine gestational sac plus a left adnexal lesion and moderate free fluid, along with hypotension/near-syncope and minimal vaginal spotting—most consistent with ectopic pregnancy; GI symptoms (vomiting/diarrhea) suggest possible gastroenteritis, while shock physiology could also reflect sepsis (though absence of fever and focal infection signs makes this less likely).

diagnano|8eaf60987b.findings: Empty uterus with β-hCG 5,180 IU/L plus a complex right adnexal mass and free fluid (with hypotension/tachycardia and RLQ tenderness) most strongly indicates a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; appendicitis is a key alternative due to RLQ tenderness/rebound, while sepsis is less likely but considered given tachycardia and low blood pressure.

diagnano|d9c24099bc.findings: Positive β-hCG (3,760 IU/L) with no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound, left adnexal mass, and moderate complex pelvic free fluid with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding is most consistent with ectopic pregnancy.

diagnano|f621ae0362.findings: Severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea, small vaginal bleeding, β-hCG ~3,760 IU/L with no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound, plus a left adnexal mass and moderate complex pelvic fluid strongly indicate ectopic pregnancy; absence of fever/WBC rise makes sepsis or alternative causes less likely but still considered given tachycardia and guarding.

diagnano|d05853d734.findings: Positive β-hCG with an empty uterus plus a complex right adnexal mass and free fluid strongly indicates ectopic pregnancy, with hypotension/tachycardia raising concern for hemorrhagic shock and possible infectious complication, while the presentation could also mimic acute appendicitis causing right iliac fossa pain.

diagnano|a2dcad0bc0.findings: Positive β-hCG (3,760 IU/L) with no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound plus left adnexal mass, moderate complex pelvic free fluid, and sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vaginal bleeding strongly suggest ectopic pregnancy.

diagnano|e8776fae07.findings: Hypotension (94/61), tachycardia (116), high β-hCG (5,180) with an empty uterus on ultrasound, and a complex right adnexal mass with free fluid strongly indicate a likely ectopic pregnancy (possible rupture/hemoperitoneum), with sepsis as a competing consideration given systemic instability and anemia, and appendicitis as a less likely alternative cause of focal right iliac fossa tenderness.

diagnano|27b09d5f52.findings: Pregnancy with β-hCG 7,420 IU/L, no intrauterine sac on bedside ultrasound, and substantial free fluid plus hypotension (88/56) with tachycardia (122) strongly indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; shock could also be confused with sepsis, and the rebound/left-sided acute abdomen warrants appendicitis as an alternative.

diagnano|6637437d76.findings: Positive β-hCG with no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound plus a left adnexal mass and moderate complex pelvic fluid with pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding strongly indicate ectopic pregnancy; appendicitis or (less likely) sepsis are alternative considerations given the abdominal tenderness and systemic symptoms but are less consistent with the imaging/β-hCG pattern.

diagnano|dcea3a5f51.findings: Positive pregnancy test with β-hCG 7,420 IU/L, bedside ultrasound showing no intrauterine sac and substantial free intraperitoneal fluid (with hypotension/tachycardia and referred shoulder pain) strongly indicates a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; persistent shock raises concern for secondary sepsis, though less likely than ectopic, with acute appendicitis a distant alternative given pelvic/abdominal tenderness.

diagnano|a19f551c95.findings: Pregnancy with β-hCG 7,420 IU/L, no intrauterine sac on bedside ultrasound, substantial free fluid/possible hemoperitoneum, and hypotension/tachycardia with acute severe unilateral pelvic pain and rebound strongly suggest a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

diagnano|872b31c55f.findings: Positive β-hCG (8,140 IU/L) with no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound plus a left adnexal mass and vaginal spotting with falling hemoglobin strongly suggest a rupturing ectopic pregnancy.

diagnano|3afe0d29d8.findings: Positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine sac on bedside ultrasound plus substantial free fluid (hemoperitoneum) and hypotension (88/56) with tachycardia (122) and anemia (Hb 8.9) strongly suggest a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; concern for systemic infection is secondary given lactate 3.1 despite afebrile status, while acute appendicitis is a less likely alternative explanation for peritoneal signs in the setting of pelvic/abdominal pain.

diagnano|775ba08817.findings: Pregnant patient with high β-hCG (8,140 IU/L), no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal US, left adnexal mass, and falling hemoglobin (9.9→9.2 g/dL) with lower abdominal pain and spotting strongly suggest ectopic pregnancy.

diagnano|2a885a3fd8.findings: Positive pregnancy hormone with no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound, left adnexal mass, scant spotting, suprapubic tenderness, and a falling hemoglobin strongly indicate ectopic pregnancy; severe ongoing symptoms with anemia also warrant considering sepsis (e.g., from threatened rupture/infection) and abdominal pathology such as acute appendicitis as secondary differentials.

diagnano|1b87f8e18e.findings: Pregnancy with rising hCG (8,140 IU/L), scant spotting, mild suprapubic tenderness, no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound, left adnexal mass, and falling hemoglobin strongly indicate ectopic pregnancy with possible ongoing bleeding.

diagnano|498ceedffa.findings: Persistent high fever for 8 days with bilateral conjunctival injection, diffuse erythema of lips/‘strawberry’-type tongue, faint reticular abdominal rash, erythematous palms/soles, cervical lymphadenopathy, marked inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, and echocardiographic pericardial effusion are most consistent with Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|24b587dcca.findings: Prolonged high fever (8 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, erythematous oral changes (erythema of lips/coated red tongue), faint truncal rash, erythematous palms/soles, unilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, and mild pericardial effusion are most consistent with Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|d618127998.findings: Prolonged high fever (8 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes (erythematous lips/coated “strawberry” tongue), polymorphous/faint truncal rash, erythematous palms/soles, cervical lymphadenopathy, marked systemic inflammation (CRP/ESR, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia), and echocardiographic involvement (pericardial effusion) strongly suggest Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|9734442d52.findings: Persistent high fever for 7 days plus conjunctival injection, dry/cracked lips with strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash involving trunk/groin, swollen hands with periungual peeling, and elevated inflammatory markers with mild coronary prominence on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|2efdca769a.findings: Eight days of high persistent fever with bilateral conjunctival injection, erythematous lips/diffuse mucosal changes (coated red tongue), faint abdominal reticular rash, erythematous palms/soles, cervical lymphadenopathy, marked inflammation (CRP/ESR) and thrombocytosis, plus echocardiographic involvement (pericardial effusion) are most consistent with Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|e236504ffc.findings: Prolonged high fever for 7 days plus all classic mucocutaneous features—bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, bright “strawberry” tongue with fissured lips, diffuse maculopapular rash, swollen hands with periungual peeling—and mild coronary involvement on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|d581e1558b.findings: Prolonged high fever (7 days) with bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, “strawberry” tongue with dry fissured lips, diffuse maculopapular rash with groin involvement, swollen hands with early periungual peeling, thrombocytosis, elevated CRP, and mild proximal coronary prominence are classic for Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|b29ffc13e3.findings: Persistent high fever for 5 days with injected conjunctiva, erythematous/cracked lips, generalized polymorphous rash, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and marked inflammation with thrombocytosis strongly support Kawasaki disease; alternative infectious causes (e.g., sepsis) are considered given fever and elevated CRP/ESR, with vomiting raising gastroenteritis as a secondary consideration despite the classic mucocutaneous findings.

diagnano|f3f0cf0e7c.findings: Persistent 7-day high fever with conjunctival injection, bright-red fissured lips/“strawberry” tongue, diffuse maculopapular rash, swollen hands with periungual peeling, thrombocytosis and coronary prominence on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; severe systemic inflammation with hypotension/capillary refill delay also raises concern for sepsis, and coronary involvement can mimic/precede myocardial ischemic injury.

diagnano|dacd68e440.findings: Prolonged 5-day high fever with injected (non-exudative) conjunctiva, cracked erythematous lips/oral changes, polymorphous rash, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild extremity edema with marked inflammation and thrombocytosis strongly suggests Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|e200eba4f6.findings: Prolonged high fever (5 days) with non-exudative conjunctival injection, erythematous/cracked lips, generalized polymorphous rash, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild extremity (feet) edema with marked inflammatory markers strongly supports Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|8842101cb1.findings: Prolonged high fever with conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips, diffuse rash, mild extremity (foot) swelling, and coronary ectasia on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; severe inflammation and leukocytosis raise concern for sepsis, while meningitis was considered due to neck discomfort but CSF shows only mild pleocytosis and negative bacterial PCR/culture.

diagnano|7d13c9a79c.findings: Prolonged high fever (6 days) with mucocutaneous findings (conjunctival injection, erythematous cracked lips, diffuse rash), extremity swelling, marked inflammation with thrombocytosis (platelets 487) and coronary ectasia on echocardiography—highly characteristic of Kawasaki disease; CSF shows low WBC with negative bacterial PCR/culture, making bacterial meningitis less likely.

diagnano|573be11d6a.findings: Prolonged fever (5 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, erythematous/cracked lips, polymorphous generalized rash, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) with reactive thrombocytosis strongly suggest Kawasaki disease; lack of focal lung findings/culture positivity lowers pneumonia and sepsis likelihood but they remain important early considerations.

diagnano|cb3fda342e.findings: Persistent high fever for 6 days with conjunctival injection, erythematous cracked lips, diffuse rash, mild peripheral (feet) swelling, marked inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR), anemia/thrombocytosis, and echocardiographic coronary ectasia—most consistent with Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|000012084d.findings: Persistent fever for 5 days with marked irritability plus bilateral conjunctival injection, dry cracked erythematous oral mucosa, faint polymorphous rash, very high CRP/ESR/WBC, and echocardiographic reduced ventricular function strongly suggests Kawasaki disease with possible myocarditis.

diagnano|00435f3a51.findings: Prolonged high fever (6 days) with classic mucocutaneous findings (conjunctival injection, erythematous cracked lips, diffuse rash, mild feet swelling), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR), leukocytosis with neutrophilia, anemia and thrombocytosis, and coronary ectasia on echocardiography—while CSF shows only mild pleocytosis with negative bacterial studies, making meningitis less likely.

diagnano|3eeee608c7.findings: Prolonged high fever (5 days) with conjunctival injection, erythematous oral mucosa/dry cracked lips, faint polymorphous rash, marked systemic inflammation (CRP/ESR, leukocytosis), and reduced ventricular function with hypotension strongly suggest Kawasaki disease with possible myocarditis; negative urine culture makes UTI less likely but sterile pyuria and elevated WBCs can mimic infection, so sepsis remains an important competing diagnosis.

diagnano|2edf809bce.findings: Prolonged high fever (5 days) with marked irritability plus classic mucocutaneous features—bilateral conjunctival injection, dry cracked erythematous oral mucosa, faint polymorphous rash—and very high inflammatory markers with cardiac involvement on echo strongly point to Kawasaki disease; severe systemic illness with hypotension and leukocytosis also raises concern for sepsis, while pneumonia is a secondary consideration despite no cough.

diagnano|bb609cb1d2.findings: Six days of high fever with bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked lips, polymorphous trunk rash, erythematous palms with mildly swollen fingers, thrombocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and echocardiographic coronary prominence with sterile low-cell aspiration strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; sepsis is a close alternative given severe fever/leukocytosis, and bacterial meningitis is considered due to marked systemic inflammation (though no classic meningeal signs are described).

diagnano|eb96110e34.findings: Prolonged fever (5 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous oral mucosa/lips, polymorphous rash, marked inflammation (very high CRP/ESR, leukocytosis), and echo evidence of cardiac involvement strongly suggest Kawasaki disease; the presentation also overlaps with systemic bacterial sepsis, and vomiting/intermittent abdominal pain could mimic gastroenteritis.

diagnano|d32cc1bf27.findings: Prolonged high fever (6 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked lips, polymorphous trunk rash, erythematous palms and mildly swollen fingers, marked inflammation (CRP/ESR), thrombocytosis, and echocardiographic coronary prominence with sterile low-cell-count joint aspiration.

diagnano|1494e0923b.findings: Prolonged high fever (~6 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked lips/mucosal changes, polymorphous trunk rash, erythematous palms/mild finger swelling, elevated inflammatory markers with thrombocytosis, and echocardiographic coronary prominence strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; sterile low-WBC joint aspiration makes septic arthritis less likely but fever with marked inflammation still warrants considering sepsis.

diagnano|9e97279643.findings: Prolonged high fever (8 days) with bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue/fissured lips, generalized rash, erythema of palms/soles, and echocardiographic coronary dilation—findings most consistent with Kawasaki disease despite sterile urine cultures.

diagnano|a16a52ece7.findings: Persistent fever for 8 days with classic mucocutaneous findings (nonpurulent bilateral conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue/fissured lips, generalized rash, erythema of palms and soles) plus marked inflammation and mild coronary dilation strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|e91fc27b76.findings: Fever for 6 days plus bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips/injected oral mucosa, polymorphous trunk rash, erythematous palms with mild finger swelling, marked inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis), and echocardiographic coronary prominence strongly support Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|7f31905529.findings: Eight days of high fever with bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue/fissured lips, diffuse rash, erythema of palms/soles, very high inflammatory markers, sterile pyuria on UA, and mild coronary artery dilation are most consistent with Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|4583140fdd.findings: Eight days of high persistent fever with nonpurulent bilateral conjunctivitis, “strawberry tongue”/fissured lips, generalized rash, erythema of palms/soles, elevated inflammatory markers, and mild coronary artery dilation strongly suggest Kawasaki disease; severe systemic illness with marked leukocytosis/CRP/ESR could also represent sepsis, while pyuria with sterile cultures makes UTI less likely but still a consideration early on.

diagnano|2fe062ad7b.findings: Prolonged fever (7 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, fissured lips/red tongue, diffuse rash, hand edema, marked inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, and mild coronary artery enlargement are most consistent with Kawasaki disease; sepsis is a key alternative in a febrile infant, with pneumonia less likely given the reported presentation and normal oxygenation.

diagnano|93c2cee7d1.findings: Persistent fever for 7 days with bilateral conjunctival injection, fissured lips/red tongue, generalized rash, mild hand edema, very high CRP/ESR/thrombocytosis/low albumin, and echocardiographic mild coronary artery enlargement strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|f3cf4f53d9.findings: Prolonged fever (7 days) with bilateral conjunctival injection, fissured lips/red tongue, diffuse rash, hand edema, marked inflammatory markers with thrombocytosis, and mild coronary artery enlargement with gallbladder wall thickening/ascites are classic for Kawasaki disease; sepsis or appendicitis are main alternatives given the fever and abdominal findings.

diagnano|ff92753213.findings: Prolonged fever (7 days) plus classic mucocutaneous findings (bilateral conjunctival injection, fissured lips/red tongue, generalized rash, hand edema), very high inflammatory markers with thrombocytosis, and echocardiography showing coronary artery enlargement strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; systemic inflammatory illness such as sepsis is a key alternative given marked leukocytosis/CRP/ESR.

diagnano|4678ace027.findings: Persistent fever ≥6 days with classic mucocutaneous findings (bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips/strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash), extremity erythema/swelling, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy with marked inflammation (CRP/ESR) strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; severe systemic infection like sepsis and less likely bacterial meningitis are key alternatives given high inflammatory markers and leukocytosis.

diagnano|87052c5c61.findings: Prolonged fever >5 days with bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked erythematous lips/strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, extremity erythema/swelling, and cervical lymphadenopathy strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; the marked inflammatory markers and cytopenia/anemia also raise concern for systemic infection (sepsis), and sterile pyuria can mimic/overlap with urinary tract infection.

diagnano|7275f8d59e.findings: Nine days of high fever with nonpurulent conjunctivitis, red fissured mouth, generalized rash, hand/finger edema, bilateral ankle swelling with sterile-appearing small effusions, marked inflammation (CRP/ESR), thrombocytosis (platelets 602k), and mild coronary artery dilation on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|06206e8a3f.findings: Persistent high fever for 6 days plus bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips/strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, and erythema/swelling of hands and feet with elevated inflammatory markers and thrombocytosis strongly indicate Kawasaki disease, with sepsis and urinary tract infection as key alternatives given the fever and inflammatory/pyuria findings.

diagnano|d066e34f30.findings: Nine days of high fever with bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, red fissured mouth, generalized rash, painful ankle swelling/mild finger edema, markedly elevated CRP/ESR with anemia and thrombocytosis, and mild coronary artery dilation on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease; severe inflammation/fever could also be from sepsis or another infectious source such as pneumonia.

diagnano|a03acf939c.findings: Persistent high fever (6 days) with nonpurulent bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips with strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and erythema/swelling of hands and feet strongly suggests Kawasaki disease; marked systemic inflammation and anemia/thrombocytosis support severe infectious/inflammatory causes such as sepsis, while sterile pyuria raises consideration of UTI.

diagnano|c73141f91f.findings: Nine days of high fever with bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, red fissured mouth, generalized rash, edema of fingers, marked inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, and coronary artery dilation on echocardiography strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|d1b60de53e.findings: Infant with diffuse wheeze and fine crackles, hyperinflation with bilateral perihilar markings on CXR, and hypoxia (SpO2 91%) with symptoms triggered by coughing supports bronchiolitis; asthma exacerbation is a close alternative, while the tachycardia/slow cap refill and decreased wet diapers raise concern for sepsis despite no focal pneumonia on imaging.

diagnano|caf331de5e.findings: In a 10-month-old, diffuse wheeze with fine crackles, hyperinflation and bilateral perihilar markings on CXR, plus viral-type symptoms with oxygen desaturation and dehydration (dry lips, fewer wet diapers, prolonged cap refill) most strongly suggest bronchiolitis; asthma exacerbation is a secondary consideration given wheeze, while systemic dehydration/tachycardia keeps sepsis on the differential despite no focal consolidation and normal lactate.

diagnano|f0aec1a0c5.findings: Nine days of high fever plus nonpurulent conjunctivitis, red fissured mouth, generalized rash, extremity (finger) edema with painful ankle swelling/refusal to walk, very high inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, and mild coronary artery dilation strongly indicate Kawasaki disease.

diagnano|e56935512b.findings: In an infant <1 year, poor feeding with repeated post-tussive vomiting, diffuse wheeze with subcostal recession, and CXR showing hyperinflation with bilateral perihilar markings (no focal consolidation) strongly suggest bronchiolitis; mild hypoxia and tachycardia also raise concern for lower respiratory infection (including early pneumonia) and possible sepsis.

diagnano|807023c9c7.findings: Infant with several days of poor feeding and post-tussive/repeated vomiting, diffuse wheeze and fine crackles with subcostal recession, O2 sat 91% RA, and CXR showing hyperinflation with bilateral perihilar markings (no focal consolidation) most strongly support bronchiolitis.

diagnano|92d1024aa2.findings: Infant with 2 days of rhinorrhea, progressive noisy breathing, diffuse crackles with expiratory wheeze, viral PCR positive for RSV, hyperinflation and bilateral peribronchial thickening on CXR, and improved oxygenation after nasal suctioning with no focal consolidation favors bronchiolitis.

diagnano|09da158560.findings: Infant with 2 days of rhinorrhea and progressively noisy breathing, diffuse crackles with scattered wheeze, viral PCR positive for RSV, CXR showing hyperinflation and bilateral peribronchial thickening without focal consolidation, and improved oxygen saturation after suctioning.

diagnano|b56e92a409.findings: Infant with 2 days of rhinorrhea, noisy breathing with nasal flaring/retractions and diffuse crackles/wheeze, CXR showing hyperinflation and bilateral peribronchial thickening without consolidation, RSV-positive PCR, and improvement in oxygenation after nasal suctioning supports bronchiolitis.

diagnano|592c5bc1b7.findings: Infant with 2 days rhinorrhea and progressively noisy breathing, diffuse fine crackles with scattered wheeze, hyperinflation and bilateral peribronchial thickening on CXR, improved O2 after suctioning, and positive RSV PCR support bronchiolitis; absence of focal consolidation makes pneumonia less likely but still considered, while expiratory wheeze and increased work of breathing overlaps with asthma exacerbation.

diagnano|e128c694fd.findings: Infant with diffuse wheeze, tachypnea with subcostal recession, hyperinflation and perihilar streaking on CXR, and relatively low inflammatory markers (WBC 9.8, CRP 4 mg/L) points most to bronchiolitis; asthma exacerbation is a close alternative given wheeze, while pneumonia is less likely due to the absence of focal consolidation and only mild CRP.

diagnano|4d535ad4ed.findings: Infant with 1 day of cough and poor feeding, diffuse wheeze with subcostal recession and hypoxia improved by low-flow O2, and CXR showing hyperinflation with perihilar streaking (no consolidation) are most consistent with bronchiolitis.

diagnano|6cb80395db.findings: Infant <1 year with cough poor feeding, diffuse wheeze, hyperinflation and perihilar streaking on CXR, and mild low-grade fever with no focal consolidation—most consistent with bronchiolitis; systemic concern is less but still considered (apnea episodes, hypotension) and pneumonia/sepsis remain in differential without focal consolidation and with low inflammatory markers.

diagnano|fd9e42c1d3.findings: In a 10-month-old with several days of cough and poor feeding plus rapid breathing, diffuse wheeze, subcostal recession, mild/low-grade temperature (37.8°C), and CXR showing hyperinflation with perihilar streaking but no consolidation, bronchiolitis is most likely; asthma exacerbation and early/occult pneumonia are the main alternatives.

diagnano|5191c6575f.findings: In a 7‑month‑old with 2 days of cough/rhinorrhea followed by wheeze/noisy breathing, mild recession, diffuse peribronchial thickening with hyperinflation on CXR, low inflammatory markers (WBC 9.5, CRP 2, procalcitonin 0.06), and preserved urine output, bronchiolitis is most likely; asthma exacerbation and early community-acquired pneumonia are the main alternatives.

diagnano|e67c9c7429.findings: An under-1-year infant in winter with 2 days of viral URI symptoms (cough, rhinorrhea), wheeze/crackles, mild recession, diffuse peribronchial thickening with hyperinflation on CXR, low inflammatory markers (WBC 9.5, procalcitonin 0.06, CRP 2), and no focal lung findings most strongly suggests bronchiolitis.

diagnano|4dc1c0a3b0.findings: Infant with 2 days of cough/rhinorrhea after household viral illness, diffuse wheeze with mild recession, low inflammatory markers (WBC 9.5, CRP 2, procalcitonin 0.06), and CXR showing mild hyperinflation with diffuse peribronchial thickening—most consistent with bronchiolitis over bacterial pneumonia or other causes of wheeze.

diagnano|064ea10d1b.findings: Infant with 2 days of cough/rhinorrhea progressing to noisy breathing, bilateral wheeze/crackles with mild recession and no focal reduced air entry, CXR showing mild hyperinflation with diffuse peribronchial thickening, and low inflammatory markers (WBC 9.5, procalcitonin 0.06, CRP 2) favor viral bronchiolitis over bacterial pneumonia.

diagnano|4db64848d8.findings: Infant with nasal congestion, intermittent tachypnea and mild recession, diffuse fine crackles, bilateral peribronchial thickening on CXR without consolidation, normal glucose/lactate, and low inflammatory markers (CRP 3 mg/L, WBC 10.1) most strongly supports bronchiolitis over bacterial pneumonia or sepsis.

diagnano|4ef8d4f75e.findings: 6-month-old with recent viral exposure, nasal congestion with intermittent tachypnea, diffuse fine crackles, mild recession, low inflammatory markers/normal WBC, and CXR showing bilateral peribronchial thickening without focal consolidation—most consistent with bronchiolitis; pneumonia/sepsis are less likely but considered due to hypoxia and respiratory distress.

diagnano|c15b61aa95.findings: Young infant with recent close exposure to URTI contacts, nasal congestion, diffuse fine crackles and mild recession, CXR showing bilateral peribronchial thickening (no consolidation), and mild hypoxemia with near-normal inflammatory markers/afebrile makes bronchiolitis most likely; pneumonia and sepsis are lower-probability alternatives given the lack of consolidation, low CRP, and no marked leukocytosis or sustained systemic toxicity.

diagnano|86d6b99416.findings: Small infant with recent close respiratory-contact exposure, diffuse fine crackles/intermittent tachypnea with mild recession, afebrile with low inflammatory markers (CRP 3 mg/L, WBC 10.1), and CXR showing bilateral peribronchial thickening without focal consolidation—most consistent with bronchiolitis; pneumonia or sepsis are less likely given the lack of consolidation and minimal lab evidence of systemic infection.

diagnano|0dc36197a4.findings: Infant has preceding coryzal symptoms with tachypnea, diffuse fine crackles and intermittent wheeze, plus CXR hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening—most consistent with bronchiolitis, with asthma exacerbation and infectious causes (e.g., sepsis) as key alternatives for apnea/pallor episodes.

diagnano|8576be47b2.findings: Following a recent viral prodrome (runny nose, cough) with episodic pallor/sweating and breathing pauses during feeds, exam shows tachypnea with diffuse fine crackles and intermittent wheeze, and CXR demonstrates hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening—most consistent with bronchiolitis.

diagnano|b74a59e6b4.findings: Infant with preceding viral URI symptoms (runny nose/cough), diffuse fine crackles with intermittent wheeze and tachypnea, and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening—most consistent with bronchiolitis; episodic pallor/sweating/pauses during feeds can occur with respiratory distress.

diagnano|8e1d563edf.findings: Infant with preceding URI symptoms (runny nose/cough), episodic pallor/sweating with apparent breathing pauses during feeds, diffuse fine crackles and intermittent wheeze with tachypnea and mild retractions, and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening strongly suggest bronchiolitis.

diagnano|e26dca734f.findings: A 5-month-old with 3 days of viral upper-respiratory symptoms (runny nose, cough), diffuse wheeze/crackles with mild recession, hyperinflation with peribronchial cuffing on CXR (no focal infiltrate), mild fever (38°C), and low WBC makes bronchiolitis most likely.

diagnano|03ecdc7e34.findings: An afebrile/mildly febrile 5-month-old with 3 days of viral prodrome (coryza, cough), diffuse crackles/wheezing with mild respiratory distress (subcostal recession, RR ~60), and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial cuffing and no lobar infiltrate—most consistent with bronchiolitis.

diagnano|cc2385efa4.findings: Infant <1 year in winter with 3 days viral symptoms, diffuse crackles/wheezing with mild respiratory distress, CXR showing hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing without focal lobar infiltrate, normal urine output, and low WBC support bronchiolitis over asthma or pneumonia.

diagnano|6ff0e72386.findings: An infant with 3 days of URI symptoms, diffuse wheeze/crackles with mild retractions, CXR showing hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing without lobar infiltrate, and no significant leukocytosis strongly supports bronchiolitis over pneumonia or other causes.

diagnano|49bc7fd0fe.findings: A 9-month infant with recent viral exposure, diffuse expiratory wheeze with fine crackles, hyperinflated chest x‑ray without focal opacity, low inflammatory markers (WBC 11.2, procalcitonin 0.08), and improvement in oxygenation/color after suctioning and humidified oxygen supports bronchiolitis over bacterial pneumonia or asthma.

diagnano|4524beddb5.findings: Infant with recent crowded-exposure history, diffuse expiratory wheeze with fine crackles and hyperinflation on CXR (no focal opacity), mild fever, and improvement in oxygenation/color after suction/humidified oxygen—most consistent with bronchiolitis; asthma exacerbation is a close alternative, while sepsis is less likely given low procalcitonin and no focal pneumonia on imaging.

diagnano|f15f16002d.findings: An infant with diffuse expiratory wheeze, nasal congestion, hyperinflated CXR without focal opacity, and rapid improvement in oxygenation/color after suctioning/humidified O2 with low inflammatory markers (WBC mildly elevated, procalcitonin 0.08) most strongly supports bronchiolitis.

diagnano|9702fbab0f.findings: Infant (9 months) with recent crowded sick contacts, diffuse expiratory wheeze, fine bilateral crackles, hyperinflation on CXR without focal opacity, low-grade temperature, and rapid improvement in oxygenation after suctioning/humidified oxygen strongly support bronchiolitis.

diagnano|bc88105ca8.findings: Infant age (5 months) with 4-day viral URI prodrome, diffuse crackles with expiratory wheeze, bilateral hyperinflation and perihilar/atelectatic opacities, and mild hypoxemia (SpO2 91% RA) most strongly support bronchiolitis.

diagnano|c93f64d873.findings: Infant <1 year with 4 days of rhinorrhea progressing to cough and feeding difficulty, diffuse crackles with expiratory wheeze, bilateral hyperinflation with patchy perihilar atelectatic opacities on CXR, and only mild fever with near-normal blood gas supports viral bronchiolitis over pneumonia or asthma.

diagnano|244d3ed04b.findings: Young (5-month) infant with several days of coryza progressing to cough and feeding difficulty, diffuse crackles with wheeze, bilateral hyperinflation with perihilar/atelectatic-appearing opacities, mild fever, and mild respiratory acidosis/near-normal pH—most consistent with bronchiolitis rather than focal bacterial pneumonia or noninfectious causes.

diagnano|c0fd3d67e7.findings: Infant with 4 days of URI symptoms progressing to cough and poor bottle intake, exam with tachypnea/head bobbing, diffuse crackles and expiratory wheeze, mild fever, and CXR showing bilateral hyperinflation with patchy perihilar (atelectatic) opacities with borderline hypoxemia.

diagnano|ba870450c7.findings: Infant (10 months) with 1 week of viral URI symptoms, diffuse crackles/expiratory wheeze, increased work of breathing (subcostal recession, nasal flaring), low-grade fever, and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial cuffing and only small atelectatic bands without lobar consolidation—most consistent with bronchiolitis; pneumonia is less likely due to lack of consolidation but remains a consideration.

diagnano|5d08bedac4.findings: Infant with 1 week viral URI symptoms followed by acute worsening respiratory distress, diffuse wheeze/crackles with nasal flaring and subcostal recession, O2 sat 90% RA, CXR showing hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing with only small atelectasis (no lobar consolidation), and mild inflammatory markers—most consistent with bronchiolitis.

diagnano|49964b0fd2.findings: Infant in summer with 1 week cough/congestion progressing to respiratory distress, diffuse wheeze/crackles with nasal flaring and moderate recession, SpO2 90% RA, and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial cuffing and only small linear atelectasis (no lobar consolidation) strongly support bronchiolitis; wheeze also raises asthma exacerbation, while mild inflammatory markers and fever warrant consideration of early/atypical community-acquired pneumonia.

diagnano|6aae8465f9.findings: Infant with 1 week of cough/congestion and acute worsening, diffuse crackles with expiratory wheeze, tachypnea/retractions, O2 sat 90% RA, and CXR showing hyperinflation with peribronchial cuffing and only small atelectasis (no lobar consolidation) best fits bronchiolitis; wheeze supports asthma-like exacerbation, while mild fever and symptoms keep early viral illness vs mild CAP on the differential despite lack of focal consolidation.

diagnano|8153a47114.findings: Recurrent cough/wheeze with bilateral expiratory wheeze and marked spirometric reversibility after bronchodilator (FEV1 1.9→2.5 L) strongly supports asthma exacerbation; concurrent weight loss and night sweats raise concern for pulmonary tuberculosis despite a non-focal CXR, while pneumonia is less likely given normal/clear radiography and low CRP.

diagnano|e94ac1c1ab.findings: Wheezing with hyperinflation and marked bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry strongly indicates asthma exacerbation; chronic cough with weight loss and night sweats in an HIV-positive patient raises concern for pulmonary tuberculosis, while recurrent wheeze with diffuse airway findings can overlap with bronchiolitis.

diagnano|a66c2353c8.findings: Recurrent cough/wheeze with bilateral expiratory wheeze and marked bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry (FEV1 1.9→2.5 L) strongly supports asthma exacerbation; night sweats and unintentional weight loss raise concern for pulmonary tuberculosis despite a non-focal/normal CXR, while bronchiolitis is a less likely alternative cause of wheeze.

diagnano|053f5c1d3c.findings: Reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry (FEV1 1.9→2.5 L) with hyperinflation and expiratory wheeze strongly supports asthma exacerbation, while HIV with 4-kg weight loss and night sweats raises concern for pulmonary tuberculosis and, less likely, lung cancer despite a negative chest radiograph.

diagnano|cd3e96582c.findings: Adult with audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration, mild recession, low oxygen saturation (91%), and markedly reduced peak flow (40% predicted) with improvement after nebulized bronchodilator and chest X-ray showing hyperinflation without focal consolidation.

diagnano|8479d5ba53.findings: Adult with rapid onset worsening breathlessness/bronchospasm after viral upper-respiratory symptoms, marked expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiration, RR 30/min, O2 sat 91% RA, and CXR showing hyperinflation without focal infiltrate; partial response to nebulized bronchodilator supports asthma over infection.

diagnano|baa03c686f.findings: Audible expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiration, increased work of breathing, peak flow ~40% predicted, hyperinflation on CXR, and partial bronchodilator response strongly indicate an acute asthma exacerbation, with pneumonia less likely given no focal opacity/effusion and minimal inflammatory markers.

diagnano|7a7420e00e.findings: History of several days of nasal congestion followed by 12 hours of worsening breathlessness with audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration, peak flow ~40% predicted, hyperinflation on CXR, and partial response to nebulized bronchodilator strongly supports an asthma exacerbation; lack of fever or focal infiltrate makes pneumonia less likely, and although MI is unlikely in this context, it remains a secondary consideration for chest tightness with tachycardia/hypoxia.

diagnano|d318b0b8e2.findings: Nocturnal onset dyspnea with diffuse expiratory wheeze, mild hypoxemia, CXR with hyperinflation, and marked improvement after inhaled bronchodilator plus systemic corticosteroids strongly indicate an asthma exacerbation; pneumonia is less likely due to afebrile status and no radiographic edema/infiltrate, and MI is unlikely given non-ischemic ECG and very low troponin.

diagnano|0498185332.findings: No fever, diffuse expiratory wheeze with hyperinflation, hypoxia (SpO₂ 92% RA), and marked improvement after inhaled bronchodilator plus systemic corticosteroids strongly support an acute asthma-type airway exacerbation; pneumonia/bronchiolitis are lower-probability alternatives given the lack of focal infectious signs.

diagnano|811683619a.findings: No fever; diffuse expiratory wheeze with hypoxia that rapidly improves after inhaled bronchodilator and systemic corticosteroid, plus CXR hyperinflation without edema or infiltrate, most strongly supports acute asthma exacerbation.

diagnano|d108ed3ce2.findings: No ischemic ECG/troponin elevation and D-dimer is low, chest X-ray shows hyperinflation (not edema/infiltrate), and there is diffuse expiratory wheeze with marked improvement after inhaled bronchodilator plus systemic corticosteroids—most consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation.

diagnano|ba3402b8b4.findings: Diffuse wheeze with prolonged expiration, improvement after bronchodilator with objective peak-flow rise (280→360 L/min), and CXR showing only mild hyperinflation with no consolidation/cavitation strongly suggest an asthma exacerbation rather than infection.

diagnano|d0848d1468.findings: Diffuse wheeze with prolonged expiration, mild hypoxia (SpO2 93%), CXR showing mild hyperinflation without consolidation, and clear bronchodilator/peak-flow response (280→360 L/min) most strongly support asthma exacerbation; pneumonia is less likely given lack of focal consolidation and low inflammatory markers, while subacute cough warrants considering pulmonary tuberculosis despite no cavitation or mass on X-ray.

diagnano|f5362bbba4.findings: Subacute progressive cough and breathlessness with diffuse wheeze/prolonged expiration, mild hyperinflation on CXR, and clear improvement in symptoms/peak flow after bronchodilator strongly suggests an asthma exacerbation rather than infection (no focal consolidation, afebrile, low CRP/WBC).

diagnano|5378263b5b.findings: Rapid onset severe breathlessness with diffuse wheeze and hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH 7.28, pCO2 52) that improved after bronchodilator, magnesium, and corticosteroids, with clear chest radiograph and no fever or focal lung findings.

diagnano|1d2a8fc4f1.findings: Rapid onset severe breathlessness with diffuse wheeze, hypoxemia with mild hypercapnia (ABG), clear chest radiograph, and clinical improvement after continuous bronchodilator plus magnesium and corticosteroid strongly support an acute asthma exacerbation over bronchiolitis or pneumonia.

diagnano|07f21c9163.findings: Three weeks of progressive cough and breathlessness with diffuse wheeze/prolonged expiration, mild hyperinflation on CXR, hypoxia on room air (SpO2 93%), and clear improvement/peak-flow improvement after bronchodilator strongly indicate an asthma exacerbation; lack of focal consolidation/cavitation and only mild inflammatory markers makes bacterial pneumonia less likely, and bronchiolitis is unlikely in an adult but remains a differential for wheeze/cough.

diagnano|c8db9425c9.findings: Rapid onset diffuse wheezing with hypoxemia and hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, pCO2 52, SpO2 86%) plus improvement after continuous bronchodilator, magnesium, and corticosteroids strongly supports an asthma exacerbation; CXR is clear and afebrile, making pneumonia/sepsis less likely, though sepsis is a consideration in the presence of vomiting/agitation.

diagnano|8e60471b5f.findings: Rapid onset severe breathlessness with diffuse wheeze, hypoxemia (SpO2 86% RA), hypercapnic acidosis on ABG (pH 7.28, pCO2 52), clear CXR, and clear clinical improvement after bronchodilators/magnesium/corticosteroids strongly suggest an asthma exacerbation; bronchiolitis is a close alternative in a young child with wheeze, while sepsis is less likely given afebrile status, lack of focal/systemic infectious features, and only mildly elevated lactate (2.1).

diagnano|d3e7008602.findings: Exercise-triggered wheeze/chest tightness with tachycardia, O2 sat 92% on room air, peak flow ~45% predicted, normal chest X-ray, and rapid improvement with inhaled bronchodilator plus corticosteroids with peak flow rising to ~78% strongly supports an asthma exacerbation over infectious causes.

diagnano|ceecf2e929.findings: Episodic cough/wheeze/chest tightness triggered by exercise with marked hypoxia (SpO2 92% RA), very low peak expiratory flow (45% predicted) that rapidly improved after inhaled bronchodilator and corticosteroid (SpO2 98%, PEF 78% predicted), with normal chest X-ray and non-diagnostic ECG/troponin.

diagnano|097da4e73a.findings: Exercise-triggered cough/wheeze/chest tightness with marked reversible airflow limitation (PEF ~45%→78% after bronchodilator + corticosteroid) and normal CXR make asthma exacerbation most likely; MI is less likely given no focal chest pain and non-diagnostic troponin, while pneumonia is unlikely with afebrile status and a normal chest radiograph.

diagnano|50b73c90f4.findings: Exercise-triggered cough/wheeze/chest tightness with hypoxia, marked reversible airflow limitation (PEF ~45% predicted improving to ~78% after inhaled bronchodilator + corticosteroid) and normal CXR strongly suggest asthma exacerbation; low troponin and rapid response make MI and pneumonia less likely but still need early consideration.

diagnano|04a9faf9d7.findings: Recurrent dry cough with nocturnal breathlessness, bilateral expiratory wheeze with mild recession, no fever/infiltrate on CXR, and objective improvement in peak expiratory flow after inhaled therapy strongly indicate asthma exacerbation.

diagnano|b75db56892.findings: Recurrent work-related dry cough with nocturnal breathlessness, bilateral expiratory wheeze/reduced air entry, no fever and normal chest X‑ray, and significant improvement in peak expiratory flow after inhaled therapy strongly support asthma exacerbation; eosinophilia further favors an allergic/reactive airway process.

diagnano|9a3674fee9.findings: Dry cough with nocturnal breathlessness, bilateral expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry, and clear improvement in peak expiratory flow after inhaled therapy (with normal CXR, no fever, and low CRP) strongly support asthma exacerbation, with pneumonia/bronchiolitis less likely given the lack of infiltrate or systemic/infectious signs.

diagnano|2095268b45.findings: No fever, normal CXR, bilateral expiratory wheeze with improved peak flow after inhaled therapy, and eosinophilia (0.62 × 10^9/L) strongly support an asthma exacerbation; absence of radiographic infiltrate makes pneumonia less likely, though it is considered in persistent cough/respiratory symptoms.

diagnano|ac6be75217.findings: Prolonged outdoor exposure with warm/dry skin, fever, tachycardia, hypoxia, and rapid improvement after cooling plus normal CXR and normal mental status point to heat stroke; prominent wheeze and marked bronchodilator response suggest concurrent asthma exacerbation; afebrile/septic source is less supported but fever with tachycardia and respiratory distress warrants considering sepsis.

diagnano|2a9d9c28d6.findings: Recent prolonged outdoor work with warm (but dry) skin, systemic symptoms (headache, weakness, nausea), fever (38.3°C), tachycardia/tachypnea with hypoxemia, and marked improvement after cooling and supportive care favor heat stroke; diffuse wheeze/breathlessness responsive to bronchodilators suggests concurrent asthma exacerbation, while infection is less supported (clear CXR, low lactate) but cannot be fully excluded.

diagnano|2a61d6fa56.findings: Heat exposure with hyperthermia (38.3°C), tachycardia and tachypnea during prolonged outdoor work, warm dry skin, and rapid improvement after cooling strongly suggest heat-related illness, with concurrent wheeze/cough responsive to bronchodilators indicating an asthma exacerbation; sepsis is less likely given normal mental status, low lactate (1.8), and clear chest radiograph but cannot be fully excluded.

diagnano|cd186580c3.findings: An adult developed breathlessness, cough, tachycardia, fever, and hypoxia after prolonged outdoor exposure with warm (initially) dry skin and rapid clinical improvement after cooling, IV fluids, and inhaled bronchodilators; clear chest radiograph and low lactate make pneumonia and severe infection less likely.

diagnano|94879899e6.findings: Diffuse expiratory wheeze with tachypnea/hypoxemia, elevated WBC/CRP, no focal opacity on CXR, and marked improvement in peak flow and oxygen saturation after inhaled bronchodilator and corticosteroid strongly indicate an acute asthma exacerbation; pneumonia/sepsis are secondary considerations given fever and inflammatory markers.

diagnano|e5b14fc427.findings: Adult with diffuse expiratory wheeeze and reduced air entry, hypoxemia (SpO2 89% RA) and significant improvement in peak flow and oxygenation after inhaled bronchodilator and corticosteroids, with no focal opacity on chest X‑ray and only low-grade fever/inflammatory markers.

diagnano|b851629b99.findings: Diffuse expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry, hypoxia (SpO2 89% RA), tachypnea, and rapid improvement in peak flow and oxygenation after inhaled bronchodilator and corticosteroid—plus no focal opacity on chest X-ray—most strongly suggest an asthma exacerbation, while fever/leukocytosis keep pneumonia or systemic infection (sepsis) on the differential.

diagnano|5ce36e0216.findings: Diffuse expiratory wheeze with tachypnea, hypoxia (SpO2 89% RA) and improvement in peak flow and oxygenation after inhaled bronchodilator plus corticosteroid, with chest X‑ray showing no focal opacity, make an acute obstructive process (asthma exacerbation) most likely over bacterial pneumonia.

diagnano|4dfcd3fb63.findings: Viral prodrome with wheeze/chest tightness, diffuse respiratory symptoms worsened over 48 hours, hypoxia (SpO2 90% RA) with markedly reduced peak expiratory flow (42% predicted), peribronchial thickening on CXR without consolidation, and improvement with repeated bronchodilators and corticosteroids supports acute airway hyperreactivity (asthma exacerbation) over bacterial pneumonia.

diagnano|14fd81b1b1.findings: Wheezing/chest tightness with low peak expiratory flow (42% predicted), peribronchial thickening without consolidation, hypoxemia (SpO2 90% RA), and improvement after repeated bronchodilators and corticosteroids strongly suggest an asthma-type lower airway exacerbation rather than focal bacterial pneumonia.

diagnano|fc1e12efd0.findings: Worsening cough/wheeze/chest tightness over 48 hours with hypoxemia (SpO2 90% RA), low peak expiratory flow (42% predicted), and clear response to inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids with CXR showing peribronchial thickening (no consolidation) most strongly supports an asthma exacerbation; viral bronchial involvement could mimic bronchiolitis, and pneumonia is less likely given the lack of consolidation and only mild inflammatory markers.

diagnano|5f4fc6ce28.findings: Cough/wheeze after a recent URI, diffuse wheeze with reduced air entry responding to inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, peribronchial thickening on CXR without consolidation, and low-grade labs (mildly elevated WBC/CRP) support asthma exacerbation over pneumonia.

diagnano|3c9a588efb.findings: This presentation is most consistent with an acute anterior STEMI: chest/back discomfort with nausea and profound new exhaustion plus ECG showing ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression, and rapidly rising high-sensitivity troponin (73 → 520 ng/L).

diagnano|026d0e56bf.findings: ST-segment elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression and a marked rise in high-sensitivity troponin over 2 hours strongly indicate an acute myocardial infarction; alternate causes are less likely given the specific ischemic ECG changes and enzyme pattern.

diagnano|ff0fefb6b3.findings: Anterior ST-segment elevations (V1–V4) with reciprocal inferior ST depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin within 2 hours strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; nausea/unwellness could overlap with GI causes, though ECG/troponin findings favor MI.

diagnano|408a531137.findings: Atypical dull interscapular pain with nausea and ECG showing anterior ST-elevation (V1–V4) with reciprocal inferior ST depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin (73 → 520 ng/L) is most consistent with acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|1ac401af34.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern (2‑mm ST elevation in II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression) plus rising high‑sensitivity troponin-T and ongoing chest discomfort strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; gastrointestinal symptoms (belching, nausea) could mimic pain, with less likely alternative causes such as migraine/functional discomfort.

diagnano|0696918d93.findings: Inferior-wall pattern ST elevation on ECG (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal depression and a dynamic rise in high-sensitivity troponin (96 → 348 ng/L) strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; GI-type symptoms (belching, nausea, burning after dinner) suggest possible gastroenteritis as a secondary consideration, while migraine is less likely but can mimic nonspecific chest discomfort.

diagnano|83bf8b22a8.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern on ECG (2-mm ST elevation in II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression) plus rising high-sensitivity troponin-T (96 to 348 ng/L) strongly indicates acute myocardial infarction despite associated nausea/belching.

diagnano|0271fc9c63.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern on ECG (2-mm ST elevation in II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression in I/aVL) plus dynamic rise in high-sensitivity troponin (96→348 ng/L) and associated diaphoresis/nausea despite normal vitals and benign abdominal exam strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|5fc1c1136e.findings: Central pressure chest pain radiating to left shoulder/jaw with diaphoresis/nausea, persistent symptoms, and ECG showing anterior ST-segment elevation with reciprocal depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin are most consistent with acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|9ab74c775d.findings: Classic ischemic chest pain (central pressure radiating to left shoulder/jaw with diaphoresis and nausea) plus ECG with anterior ST-segment elevation (V2–V5) and rising high-sensitivity troponin confirm acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|f41206e259.findings: Central pressure radiating to left shoulder/jaw with diaphoresis and nausea, persistent pain, hypertension/tachycardia, and ECG showing anterior ST-segment elevation (V2–V5) with reciprocal depression plus markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin.

diagnano|7849ed2305.findings: Central pressure radiating to left shoulder/jaw with diaphoresis, nausea, persistent symptoms, hypertension/tachycardia, and ECG showing ST-segment elevation (V2–V5) with reciprocal depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate an acute STEMI; nausea could mimic GI illness, while absence of fever/infection signs makes sepsis less likely.

diagnano|bd203974f5.findings: 52-year-old with sudden diaphoresis/near-syncope, hypoxemia, and ECG showing ST elevation in V2–V5 with reciprocal depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; lack of fever/cough makes infection less likely but sepsis or an atypical lower respiratory infection remain secondary considerations for dyspnea and lactate elevation.

diagnano|33b695b3c5.findings: ST-elevation on ECG in V2–V5 with reciprocal depression, rising high-sensitivity troponin-T, tachycardia/diaphoresis and near-syncope strongly indicate an acute MI; persistent tachypnea with mildly elevated lactate keeps sepsis and an infectious respiratory process on the differential despite no fever/cough and clear lung exam.

diagnano|7f0e1e72e9.findings: Sudden dyspnea with pulmonary edema plus ST-elevation in V1–V4 and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate an acute myocardial infarction (with hypoxemia and lactate supporting systemic stress).

diagnano|ab2e0fe7eb.findings: ST-segment elevation in V1–V4 with rising high-sensitivity troponin, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and chest X-ray showing pulmonary edema strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; ongoing systemic findings (cool/clammy, lactate 3.1) keep sepsis in consideration, while absence of fever and lack of focal consolidation make pneumonia less likely but possible.

diagnano|d8b049806a.findings: ST-segment elevation in V2–V5 with reciprocal depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin is most consistent with an acute myocardial infarction; alternative causes are less likely given no fever/cough and normal exam, though tachycardia with mildly elevated lactate (and hypoxemia) could suggest systemic infection or, less likely, atypical pneumonia.

diagnano|b91aa8ac7f.findings: ST-segment elevation in V1–V4 with rising high-sensitivity troponin-T, frequent ventricular ectopy, and pulmonary edema/BNP elevation strongly suggest acute myocardial infarction; persistent tachycardia with elevated lactate could reflect sepsis, and hypoxic respiratory symptoms with a dry cough keep community-acquired pneumonia on the differential despite no focal consolidation or fever.

diagnano|2926af8ed9.findings: Sudden dyspnea with hypoxia and pulmonary edema plus ECG ST elevation in V1–V4 with markedly rising troponin and ventricular ectopy strongly indicates acute MI causing cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

diagnano|4b41f03cdd.findings: Severe diaphoresis with near-syncope, marked tachycardia/tachypnea, and ECG ST-elevation in V2–V5 with reciprocal depression plus rising high-sensitivity troponin-T strongly indicate an acute myocardial infarction; lactate elevation supports possible systemic illness, and pneumonia is a less likely alternative despite no cough/fever and clear lungs.

diagnano|02e6a0a7f1.findings: Crushing substernal chest pain with diaphoresis and radiation to the left arm, ongoing >30 minutes, ECG with ST-elevation (V2–V6 and I) plus reciprocal inferior depression, and rising high-sensitivity troponin (61→487 ng/L) strongly indicate an acute STEMI.

diagnano|95a3d47494.findings: Central crushing substernal pain radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis, ST-elevation in V2–V6 and I with reciprocal inferior depression, and rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate an acute MI.

diagnano|bc9a8c4816.findings: Crushing substernal pain with diaphoresis and left arm radiation plus ST-segment elevation in V2–V6/I with reciprocal inferior depression and rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate an acute STEMI; lack of fever or infectious signs makes sepsis/pneumonia less likely.

diagnano|553441122b.findings: Prolonged crushing substernal chest pain with radiation to the left arm plus ECG with ST elevation (V2–V6 and I) and reciprocal depression, and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin are diagnostic for acute STEMI.

diagnano|df3bb34bf0.findings: Retrosternal squeezing discomfort at rest with diaphoresis/anxiety, ischemic ECG changes (ST depression V4–V6, T inversion I/aVL) and rising high-sensitivity troponin-T are most consistent with an acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI/MI), while other causes are less likely given afebrile status, clear lungs, and absence of infectious or neurologic features.

diagnano|699e8a3dac.findings: Retrosternal squeezing pain at rest with sympathetic features, dynamic ischemic ECG changes (ST depression V4–V6, T-wave inversion I/aVL), and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|6f14177d91.findings: Inferior ST-segment elevation (II/III/aVF) with complete heart block, bradycardia (HR ~38–54), hypotension, and rapidly rising high-sensitivity troponin with no fever or infectious focus most strongly indicate an acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|fd5c013bbe.findings: Resting retrosternal pressure radiating to both arms with anxiety/pallor/diaphoresis plus ischemic ECG changes (ST depression V4–V6, T-wave inversion I/aVL) and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin (178→536 ng/L) strongly indicate an acute coronary syndrome/acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|b95693da6c.findings: Definitive ACS features with classic retrosternal pressure at rest, anxiety/diaphoresis, dynamic ECG ischemic changes (ST depression V4–V6, T inversion I/aVL) and rising high-sensitivity troponin-T (178→536 ng/L) strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|7176477cf2.findings: Substernal/back interscapular dull ache with nausea/unusual exhaustion plus ECG showing anterior ST-elevation (V1–V4) with reciprocal inferior ST depression and rising high-sensitivity troponin indicates acute myocardial infarction; vitals are stable and there are no infectious or GI-specific features to better explain the presentation.

diagnano|8f3430833c.findings: Inferior ST-segment elevation (II, III, aVF) with complete heart block, bradycardia, and rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; alternatives considered are heat-related collapse (outdoor exposure) and systemic illness/sepsis given pallor/clamminess and collapse, though no fever or infectious findings are documented.

diagnano|8eac43a135.findings: 57-year-old with inferior ST-elevation (II, III, aVF), complete heart block with marked bradycardia (HR 38–54), and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin (240 → 1,020 ng/L) strongly indicates acute myocardial infarction, while alternative causes of collapse (e.g., heat-related illness or infection/sepsis) are less supported by afebrile status and lack of infectious/heat exposure vitals.

diagnano|3855c4c505.findings: Anterior STEMI pattern (ST elevation V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior depression) plus rising high-sensitivity troponin (73→520 ng/L) and atypical symptoms (nausea, exhaustion) strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|5990e2fee8.findings: Inferior ST-segment elevation (II, III, aVF) with complete heart block and rising high-sensitivity troponin strongly indicate acute myocardial infarction; hypotension with syncope broadens consideration to other causes of shock such as ectopic pregnancy or sepsis, though there are no infectious/fever findings here.

diagnano|99bea25f89.findings: Anterior chest/epigastric discomfort with nausea and marked dynamic rise in high-sensitivity troponin plus ECG showing ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression strongly indicates an acute myocardial infarction.

diagnano|d1f78314a0.findings: ST-elevation on ECG in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression and markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin are most consistent with an acute anterior STEMI; lack of fever/respiratory findings makes sepsis or pneumonia less likely, and nausea/exhaustion could be mimicked by gastrointestinal illness but does not explain the ischemic ECG/troponin pattern.

diagnano|243b4ee0aa.findings: Markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin with inferior ST elevation (II/III/aVF) and reciprocal depression plus tachycardia most strongly indicate an acute myocardial infarction; vomiting/epigastric discomfort after catered food supports gastroenteritis, and ongoing systemic illness is possible but less likely given normal temperature and only mildly elevated lactate.

diagnano|2e151ab996.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern on ECG (2-mm ST elevation in II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression), markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin (144 to 902 ng/L), and supportive symptoms (epigastric pain with vomiting) make acute myocardial infarction most likely despite normal lipase and afebrile status.

diagnano|e2f0e1cd31.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern on ECG (2-mm ST elevation II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression in aVL) with rapidly rising high-sensitivity troponin (144 → 902 ng/L) and absence of alternative primary findings like pancreatitis; epigastric pain and vomiting can mimic GI illness, with sepsis less supported by normal temperature and mild lactate (2.0).

diagnano|4f81942239.findings: Subacute (3-week) cough with intermittent fever/hemoptysis, hypoxemia, very high CRP, and CT showing innumerable uniform tiny bilateral lung nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and small pleural effusion strongly support pulmonary tuberculosis over other causes.

diagnano|96f99b7952.findings: Inferior STEMI pattern on ECG (2-mm ST elevation II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression in aVL) plus markedly rising high-sensitivity troponin (144 → 902 ng/L) with tachycardia strongly indicates acute myocardial infarction, while epigastric pain and repeated vomiting could mimic GI illness (gastroenteritis); systemic infection is less likely given normothermia and only mildly elevated lactate.

diagnano|97ae9616ee.findings: Subacute (3-week) cough with intermittent fever and small hemoptysis plus high CRP, and CT showing innumerable tiny fairly uniform bilateral lung nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and pleural effusion—classic for miliary tuberculosis.

diagnano|f952c4b088.findings: Subacute course with intermittent fever, small-volume hemoptysis, hypoxemia, markedly elevated CRP, bilateral fine crackles with mild clubbing, and CT showing innumerable uniform tiny lung nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and small pleural effusion strongly suggest miliary tuberculosis.

diagnano|c0b83f0031.findings: Subacute course with intermittent fever and small hemoptysis plus CT showing innumerable, fairly uniform bilateral pulmonary nodules (miliary pattern), mediastinal lymphadenopathy, mild hypoxia, and digital clubbing strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|ff9df3713e.findings: Subacute (2-month) intermittent fever, night sweats, weight/fatigue, chronic cough with diffuse tiny pulmonary nodules, necrotic abdominal lymph nodes, splenomegaly, ascites, and cytopenias with markedly elevated CRP strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis; systemic inflammatory illness could represent sepsis, with pneumonia as an alternative.

diagnano|29ba4f30b4.findings: Chronic (2 months) intermittent fever/night sweats, exposure to a relative with chronic cough, diffuse tiny pulmonary nodules on CT plus necrotic abdominal nodes, splenomegaly, ascites, and inflammatory markers with pancytopenia are most consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|2eb992ab20.findings: Subacute course over 2 months with night sweats/fever, hypoxia (SpO2 93%), pancytopenia, elevated CRP, and CT showing diffuse tiny pulmonary nodules plus necrotic abdominal lymph nodes, splenomegaly, and ascites strongly suggest miliary/disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|d0f39e5eff.findings: Subacute 2-month fever/night sweats, profound fatigue with pancytopenia, splenomegaly, elevated CRP/alkaline phosphatase, and CT findings of diffuse tiny pulmonary nodules plus necrotic abdominal nodes and small ascites strongly suggest disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis over the other options.

diagnano|61f7e0fb05.findings: Chronic painful, warm right knee effusion with lymphocyte-predominant synovial fluid (82% lymphocytes), very high WBC count with low synovial glucose (2.4 mmol/L), negative routine bacterial culture, systemic symptoms/night sweats, and a small apical lung opacity suggest tuberculous disease (TB arthritis with possible pulmonary TB), with septic arthritis and broader sepsis as key alternatives.

diagnano|45a57c76fc.findings: Chronic painful warm right knee with moderate effusion and aspiration showing straw-colored fluid with marked leukocytosis (18,500/µL) dominated by lymphocytes (82%) plus very high CRP and low pleural/knee fluid glucose, negative routine bacterial culture, and a small apical lung opacity in a patient with night sweats/cough exposure strongly suggest tuberculous septic arthritis with underlying pulmonary tuberculosis, with systemic sepsis less likely but possible given fever and inflammatory markers.

diagnano|8f7adba45b.findings: Chronic monoarticular warm effusion with restrictive motion, straw-colored aspirate with very high leukocytes that are predominantly lymphocytic (82%) and low glucose (2.4 mmol/L) plus intermittent fever/night sweats and an apical lung opacity with TB exposure strongly suggest tuberculous involvement, presenting as septic arthritis/tuberculous arthritis with systemic inflammatory response.

diagnano|65d24e5e55.findings: Recent travel with household TB exposure plus constitutional symptoms (weight loss, low-grade fever), severe inflammatory markers (CRP 95), anemia/hypoalbuminemia, and CT findings of terminal ileum/cecum concentric thickening with necrotic lymph nodes and ascites strongly suggest intestinal tuberculosis, with sepsis as an immediate concern given systemic inflammation.

diagnano|82e98d7ce8.findings: Chronic (4-week) warm, moderate effusion with restricted flexion and high synovial leukocytes (18,500/µL) plus very low synovial glucose (2.4 mmol/L), with negative routine bacterial culture and an apical opacity on chest x-ray, strongly suggest infection due to septic arthritis—most likely from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

diagnano|5ab7396ba4.findings: Recent travel/exposure to relatives with prolonged cough and weight loss, progressive anorexia/weight loss, high CRP with anemia/hypoalbuminemia, and CT findings of terminal ileum/cecum concentric thickening with necrotic lymph nodes and small ascites are most consistent with intestinal tuberculosis (disseminated from pulmonary TB).

diagnano|5c0130e577.findings: Prolonged fever with night sweats and dry cough with hypoxemia, high inflammatory markers, exposure to a coworker who coughed blood, and CT showing randomly distributed nodules with necrotic mediastinal nodes and small pericardial effusion strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis, with physiologic derangement consistent with sepsis.

diagnano|33f29f3fa5.findings: Ileocecal (terminal ileum/cecum) concentric thickening with necrotic regional lymph nodes, small-volume ascites, constitutional symptoms with weight loss and exposure history strongly suggest intestinal TB rather than an acute surgical or simple infectious gastroenteritis process.

diagnano|4fc9147aaa.findings: Ten days of loose stools with CT evidence of terminal ileum/cecum concentric thickening plus necrotic regional lymph nodes and ascites suggests an infectious granulomatous process (most consistent with tuberculosis) rather than uncomplicated appendicitis; systemic inflammation (fever, anemia, high CRP) raises concern for sepsis/complicated infection.

diagnano|7a41c4272d.findings: Sustained fever with night sweats and close TB exposure (coworker coughing blood), diffuse randomly distributed micronodular lung findings with necrotic mediastinal nodes and small pericardial effusion strongly indicate pulmonary tuberculosis; marked hypotension (94/58), tachycardia, lactate elevation (3.1) and confusion suggest sepsis as a complication, with community-acquired pneumonia as an alternative infectious cause.

diagnano|41fe6c9570.findings: Prolonged fever/night sweats with healthcare exposure to a coughing-blood coworker plus hypoxia and imaging showing randomly distributed nodules with necrotic mediastinal nodes and a small pericardial effusion strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis, with systemic deterioration (hypotension, tachycardia, lactate elevation, confusion) consistent with sepsis; bacterial community-acquired pneumonia is a secondary consideration given the febrile respiratory presentation and diffuse crackles.

diagnano|246a7c5ca3.findings: Prolonged fever/night sweats with diffuse bilateral micronodular/randomly distributed nodules, necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes, small pericardial effusion, hypoxemia, and sepsis physiology (hypotension, tachycardia, elevated lactate and inflammatory markers) strongly suggest miliary pulmonary tuberculosis with systemic sepsis.

diagnano|965cbdd5d1.findings: Subacute (5-week) headache with nausea, mild papilledema and communicating hydrocephalus with basal leptomeningeal enhancement plus small ring-enhancing intracranial lesions strongly suggests a chronic meningitic/infectious process, most consistent with tuberculosis-related CNS infection; inflammatory markers are elevated (CRP 39 mg/L) with intermittent low-grade fever.

diagnano|19b2704444.findings: Subacute (5-week) unilateral headache with nausea, mild fever, papilledema, MRI showing communicating hydrocephalus with basal leptomeningeal enhancement and ring-enhancing lesions, plus elevated CRP and hyponatremia, is most consistent with CNS tuberculous infection (tuberculous meningitis/tuberculomas), with bacterial meningitis and systemic infection as close alternatives.

diagnano|1bee654381.findings: Subacute 5-week course with intermittent fever, weight loss, hyponatremia, high CRP, and MRI showing communicating hydrocephalus with basal leptomeningeal enhancement and ring-enhancing lesions strongly suggest tuberculous meningitis with CNS tuberculomas (most consistent among the provided options), with bacterial meningitis and systemic sepsis as key alternatives.

diagnano|fc78bc288e.findings: Subacute (6-week) cough/low-grade fever with hoarseness, firm enlarged supraclavicular/cervical nodes, elevated CRP, and CT findings of necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes plus clustered tree-in-bud opacities with a hilar mass-like opacity strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis over other causes.

diagnano|cbe7772827.findings: Subacute 5-week headache with intermittent low-grade fever, mild papilledema/communicating hydrocephalus, basal leptomeningeal enhancement, and multiple small ring-enhancing lesions strongly suggests chronic granulomatous meningitis—most consistent with tuberculosis (tuberculous meningitis/tuberculomas), with bacterial meningitis and systemic infection as secondary considerations.

diagnano|ee36753150.findings: Subacute low-grade fever and cough with hoarseness, firm supraclavicular/cervical lymphadenopathy, and imaging showing necrotic mediastinal nodes with clustered tree-in-bud opacities strongly favor pulmonary tuberculosis over pneumonia or malignancy.

diagnano|1d85b61759.findings: Six-week history of low-grade fever and persistent cough with hoarseness/anorexia plus firm supraclavicular/cervical lymphadenopathy and imaging showing necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes with clustered tree-in-bud opacities (highly suggestive of pulmonary TB).

diagnano|f1fa5f7de8.findings: Subacute (7-week) cough with intermittent fever, minimal response to oral antibiotics, rust-colored sputum, and imaging showing dense left-upper-lobe consolidation with volume loss/cavitary lucencies plus enlarged hilar lymph nodes are most consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|11571070c2.findings: Chronic (7-week) cough with intermittent fever, very high CRP, minimal response to antibiotics, and imaging showing dense left-upper-lobe air-space opacity with volume loss, small lucencies (cavitation) and enlarged hilar lymph nodes strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|dc10cf69be.findings: Six-week history of cough/low-grade fever with hoarseness and fatigue, firm supraclavicular/cervical adenopathy, CXR/CT showing left hilar mass-like opacity, necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes, and clustered tree-in-bud opacities are most consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis; lung cancer with nodal necrosis and post-obstructive/secondary infection is the main alternative, with community-acquired pneumonia less likely given the chronic course and necrotic nodal pattern.

diagnano|698fcb13ea.findings: Prolonged (7-week) cough with intermittent fever and minimal response to antibiotics plus unilateral left-upper-lobe consolidation with volume loss, small lucencies, and enlarged hilar lymph nodes strongly suggest pulmonary tuberculosis, with community-acquired pneumonia or malignancy as important alternatives.

diagnano|d87e6389ab.findings: 7-week cough with intermittent fever, rust-colored sputum, dense left-upper-lobe air-space opacity with volume loss and small lucencies (possible cavitation) plus enlarged hilar lymph nodes, and minimal response to oral antibiotics, strongly suggest pulmonary TB; persistent localized pneumonia or malignancy are key alternatives.

diagnano|2ac580736e.findings: Subacute low-grade fever, dry cough with TB risk exposure (roommate with prolonged cough/weight loss), CT showing upper-lobe nodularity and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, and inflammatory markers (CRP 128 mg/L) with pericarditis features (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression and moderate pericardial effusion with early RA collapse) most strongly support pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|27a97958eb.findings: Subacute (3-week) low-grade fever with dry cough and reported TB contact, marked inflammatory markers (CRP 128 mg/L, anemia), upper-lobe nodularity with mediastinal lymphadenopathy on CT, and ECG showing diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression consistent with pericarditis due to TB.

diagnano|97f565e861.findings: Subacute fever with CRP elevation plus ECG typical of acute pericarditis (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression), moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with early RA diastolic collapse, and chest CT showing upper-lobe nodularity with enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes strongly suggest tuberculous involvement.

diagnano|0c86e3a1e0.findings: Subacute low-grade fever with dry cough and presumed exposure to a housemate with prolonged cough/weight loss, anemia and very high CRP, upper-lobe nodularity with enlarged mediastinal nodes on CT, plus ECG (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression) and a moderate pericardial effusion with early right-atrial diastolic collapse—most consistent with tuberculous pericarditis secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnano|d0699be83d.findings: Subacute (3-week) meningitic illness with neck stiffness, photophobia/encephalopathy, CT basal meningeal enhancement with mild hydrocephalus, and CSF showing lymphocyte predominance, high opening pressure (31 cmH₂O), low glucose (1.8 mmol/L) and elevated protein (2.4 g/L) most strongly suggests tuberculous meningitis (in the context of recent prolonged cough exposure).

diagnano|4024cda0a1.findings: Subacute (3-week) meningitis with neck stiffness, cloudy CSF with lymphocyte predominance, low CSF glucose (1.8 mmol/L) and elevated protein, high inflammatory markers, and CT basal meningeal enhancement with mild hydrocephalus is most consistent with tuberculous meningitis (listed as Pulmonary tuberculosis), with bacterial meningitis and sepsis as key alternatives.

diagnano|a8f5e47b95.findings: Subacute (3-week) meningitis picture with basal meningeal enhancement, lymphocyte-predominant cloudy CSF, low CSF glucose, elevated opening pressure (31 cmH2O), and high CRP with hyponatremia strongly suggests TB meningitis (from pulmonary TB) over typical bacterial meningitis.

diagnano|d30b2a94ae.findings: Severe hyperglycemia with metabolic acidosis (glucose 23.7 mmol/L, pH 7.21, HCO3 12, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.0) plus tachypnea, vomiting and leukocytosis with fever suggests DKA, with possible infectious trigger (cough/pleuritic pain, mild CXR changes) raising concern for pneumonia and/or sepsis.

diagnano|0fa66e7b2e.findings: Marked metabolic acidosis with low venous pH (7.21), low bicarbonate (12 mmol/L), elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate (5.0 mmol/L), and severe hyperglycemia (23.7 mmol/L) with intercurrent infection symptoms (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, elevated lactate) and mild inflammatory CXR changes consistent with a likely respiratory source.
